name: Nelumbonaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach American lotus as convergent in aquatic habit with water lilies but structurally distinct: centrally peltate leaves, emergent flowers, numerous stamens, and separate carpels embedded in an enlarged flat-topped receptacle that becomes the unmistakable showerhead fruit.

project_scope.note: Nelumbo lutea is accepted by current Kew and its native range includes Texas.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Look at the center of a leaf. The petiole attaches to the middle of the blade, making the leaf truly peltate. Then inspect the flower center for the broad flat-topped receptacle with separate pistils sunk into pits.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Perennial rhizomatous aquatic herb with conspicuous air spaces. Leaves arise directly from the rhizome on long petioles; blades are large, round and centrally peltate, floating or more often held above water.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Large solitary bisexual flowers held above the water. Tepals and stamens are numerous. Pistils are numerous and separate, each embedded individually in the expanded flat top of a turbinate receptacle.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Each carpel matures into a hard nutlike one-seeded fruit loose in its own cavity of the enlarged receptacle, producing the familiar showerhead/seedpod structure.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Round centrally peltate leaf + emergent flower + showerhead receptacle = Nelumbonaceae/Nelumbo.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: peltate leaf → water-shedding surface → emergent flower → receptacle + separate pistils → mature showerhead fruit → water-lily comparison → phylogeny surprise
visual_lesson.intro: Lotus looks like a water-lily from across a pond, but one glance at the leaf center or fruit tells you it is a completely different family—and even a different major lineage.

steps.title: 1 · Find the petiole in the middle
steps.look_for: Petiole attaches centrally on the blade rather than at a basal notch.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the fastest visual split from Nymphaeaceae.

steps.title: 2 · Watch water bead and roll
steps.look_for: Water droplets bead strongly on the waxy leaf surface.
steps.why_it_matters: Memorable surface behavior reinforces the lotus leaf identity, though it is not the sole family character.

steps.title: 3 · Find the receptacle inside the flower
steps.look_for: A broad, flattened, cone/turbine-shaped yellow receptacle with many separate stigmas/pistils embedded in pits.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the structure that later becomes the showerhead fruit.

steps.title: 4 · Follow each pit into a separate fruit
steps.look_for: Each pit contains one independent nutlike fruit rather than all carpels fusing into one ovary.
steps.why_it_matters: Makes the distinctive fruit architecture botanically understandable.

steps.title: 5 · Compare leaves with Nymphaeaceae
steps.look_for: Lotus = peltate central attachment and often emergent bowl-shaped blade; water-lily = petiole enters at basal sinus/notch.

steps.title: 6 · The phylogeny surprise
steps.look_for: Nelumbo is in Proteales, not Nymphaeales. Similar pond habit is convergence, not close relationship.
steps.why_it_matters: Turns a common visual confusion into an evolutionary learning moment.

comparisons.title: Nelumbonaceae vs Nymphaeaceae
comparisons.rule: Lotus has centrally peltate leaves and separate carpels embedded in a showerhead receptacle. Water-lilies attach the petiole at a basal sinus and lack the lotus receptacle.

comparisons.title: Nelumbonaceae vs Ceratophyllaceae
comparisons.rule: Lotus is rooted in sediment with huge emergent/floating peltate leaves and showy flowers. Ceratophyllum is rootless, completely submerged and has tiny naked flowers.

visual_lesson.caveat: The dry lotus 'pod' is an enlarged receptacle holding separate fruits, not one capsule. Also, lotus and water-lilies are not close relatives despite their shared aquatic habit.

genera.fast_cue: centrally peltate round leaf + emergent many-stamen flower + showerhead receptacle

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Accepted by current Kew; native range includes Texas.
